There Are No Dumb Questions Q: Why expand 6 clues into 64 numbers when 6 numbers already sound like enough? A: Because scams hide in the combination of clues (for example, spending big at 3:00 AM plus impossible 900 km/h travel). Expanding into 64 dimensions with sine/cosine waves and cross-products lets a simple angle comparison inside the database spot those curved combinations without calling a heavy neural network! Q: Does the database freeze while waiting ~3.5 seconds for Gemini? A: Never! In Phase 1 (< 2 ms), the worker marks the row 'PROCESSING' and closes the database transaction before calling Gemini. While Gemini thinks in the cloud, zero rows are locked and live payments keep flying through. Bullet Points (Section 3 Math in 3 Lines) 6 clues → 64 numbers (length 1.0): turns behavior into a directional arrow ready for angle checks inside the database. 0.92 circuit breaker: stops a brand-new mule account from slipping past with zero 24-hour spending history. Gemini vaccine (~3.5 s offline): investigates grey-zone cases with zero DB locks and writes the new signature with >= 0.98 deduplication. 4. What Is Analyzed in the Benchmark? (p50, p95, p99, Recall@10, and Buffer Hit Ratio) When we compare Google Cloud AlloyDB and AWS Aurora PostgreSQL 16, we never rely on a simple "average" response time. Averages hide tail spikes: if 99 payments finish in 5 milliseconds and 1 payment freezes for 5 full seconds, the average looks fine, even though customers are experiencing timeouts. Instead, our benchmark runner (src/benchmark/runner.py) analyzes five concrete metrics on every run: p50 Latency (The Median Customer): Imagine lining up 100 payments from fastest (#1) to slowest (#100). p50 is the time of payment #50 right in the middle. When p50 = 5.60 ms (local AlloyDB Omni) or 26.71 ms (4-vCPU cloud stress test at 486 TPS), half of all payments finished in that time or less. p95 Latency (Peak Traffic Stability): p95 is payment #95 in that line of 100. When p95 = 9.09 ms (local AlloyDB Omni) or 73.99 ms (4-vCPU cloud stress test), 95 out of every 100 payments finished in that time or less. p99 Latency (The Worst-Case 1% Tail That Central Banks Enforce): p99 is payment #99 out of 100, representing the slowest 1% of requests when the database is under full 500 TPS stress. Instant payment networks like PIX enforce strict service-level agreements on p99. Recall@10 (Scam Detection Accuracy): After the load test, the runner executes filtered vector queries twice: once using the vector index (alloydb_scann or pgvector HNSW), and once with indexes turned off (SET LOCAL enable_indexscan = off) so PostgreSQL checks every row to find the true 10 closest fraud vectors. Recall@10 is the overlap between the two lists: 1.00 means the index caught 10 out of the 10 real frauds, whereas 0.67 means the index missed roughly 1 in 3 real frauds. Shared Buffer Hit Ratio (RAM Efficiency): Measured directly from PostgreSQL's pg_stat_database catalog (blks_hit vs. blks_read), showing what percentage of page reads came straight from RAM without touching disk storage. Bullet Points (How to Read Any Benchmark Like a Pro) Ignore simple averages: always look at p99 — it tells you whether the unluckiest 1% of customers are stuck waiting at the checkout counter. Speed without accuracy is useless: answering in 5 ms doesn't help if Recall@10 is 0.67 and 1 out of every 3 real scams slips through the net! 5. Which Database Performed Better, and Why? To guarantee a 100% fair race, both managed cloud clusters ran the exact same version (PostgreSQL 16.14) and identical hardware capacity (4 vCPU / 32 GB RAM — 32 GiB in AWS binary notation). If a single AlloyDB query took ~5.1 ms, why is p99 in the cloud table 95.54 ms? A: Picture a supermarket cashier who scans your items in 5 seconds. If 1 shopper arrives at a time, you're out in 5 seconds! Q: How did alloydb_scann get faster when the SQL filter got stricter (212.31 ms at 50% → 95.54 ms at 0.5%)? A: Because bitmap pre-filtering shrinks the pile before measuring any vector angles! It's like hunting for a rare trading card: if someone first hands you only the 2,500 holographic cards (0.5%) instead of 250,000 (50%), you find the right one way faster — and without missing a single match (100% Recall@10). 5.4 Four "Aha!" Engineering Clues Discovered on Managed AlloyDB Beginner Note: This subsection is an optional deep dive for database engineers (DBAs). If you are new to databases, feel free to jump straight to Section 5.5 (Costs) without missing a beat! Running the full 2.5M-row benchmark on managed Google Cloud AlloyDB 16.14 surfaced four practical tweaks that delivered a 12.7x per-query speedup: Use now(), never clock_timestamp(), in Columnar Engine filters: The Trap: clock_timestamp() is VOLATILE (re-evaluated per row), blocking SIMD pushdown. The Fix & Payoff: Switching to now() - INTERVAL '24 hours' (STABLE) unlocked "Columnar cache search mode": "native". Split COUNT(DISTINCT) out of the columnar aggregation (12.7x speedup): The Trap: Counting distinct devices inside the 40,050-row scan forced a 3.4 MB in-memory quicksort (64.8 ms). The Fix & Payoff: Splitting sql/queries/hot_path_authorize.sql into corridor_stats (pure SIMD AVG in 4.24 ms, 0 shared buffer hits) + sender_velocity (Index Only Scan in 0.11 ms) cut isolated query time to ~5.1 ms. Set scann.vector_node_min_dimensionality = 32 for 64-D vectors: The Trap: Single-stage bitmap pre-filtering defaults to vectors with >= 100 dimensions. The Fix & Payoff: Setting min_dimensionality = 32 + custom_scan_replace_prefilter = on unlocked Bitmap assisted pre-filtering in 0.29 ms at 100% Recall@10. Run VACUUM ANALYZE before populating the Columnar Engine: The Trap: Bulk COPY rows must be marked all-visible to load 100% into columnar stripes. The Fix & Payoff: VACUUM ANALYZE loaded 96,777 / 96,777 blocks into columnar stripes; on managed AlloyDB, use ALTER DATABASE ... SET (instead of ALTER SYSTEM SET) and google_ml.create_model(..., model_auth_type => 'alloydb_service_agent_iam'). 5.5 Cost Analysis (FinOps): What Each Scenario Costs (Made Crystal Clear!) Creates the shared B-Tree indexes (idx_ledger_velocity_btree, idx_ledger_sender_24h, and idx_fraud_sig_filters) and builds idx_fraud_sig_scann: CREATE INDEX idx_fraud_sig_scann ON fraud_signatures USING scann (behavioral_vec cosine) WITH (num_leaves = 100, quantizer = 'sq8');. Configures 8 database-level SCaNN parameters via ALTER DATABASE postgres SET (including scann.vector_node_min_dimensionality = 32, scann.custom_scan_replace_prefilter = on, scann.num_leaves_to_search = 15, and scann.pre_reordering_num_neighbors = 50) to enable single-stage bitmap pre-filtering (Custom Scan (vector scan)), and calls SELECT google_columnar_engine_add('public.payment_ledger', ...) to pin the analytical columns in the SIMD columnar cache. sql/03_setup_aurora_baseline.sql: Fair AWS Aurora Baseline Creates the identical relational B-Tree indexes (idx_ledger_velocity_btree and idx_ledger_sender_24h) on payment_ledger, drops idx_fraud_sig_filters (DROP INDEX IF EXISTS) so Aurora evaluates true HNSW post-filtering, and builds the pgvector HNSW index (USING hnsw (behavioral_vec vector_cosine_ops) WITH (m = 16, ef_construction = 64)) on fraud_signatures. sql/queries/hot_path_authorize.sql: Inside the 5-Stage Single-Trip CTE Stage 1 (corridor_stats + sender_velocity -> velocity_window): Separates the 24-hour corridor average (corridor_stats using now() - INTERVAL '24 hours' for pure SIMD Columnar Engine aggregate pushdown) from the sender's individual 24-hour velocity (sender_velocity using Index Only Scan on idx_ledger_sender_24h for sum_24h_cents, tx_count_24h, and distinct_devices_24h). Stage 2 (vector_anomaly): Queries fraud_signatures with WHERE merchant_category = $3 AND selectivity_bucket <= $4 ORDER BY behavioral_vec <=> $2::vector(64) LIMIT 10, converting cosine distance into similarity 1.0 - distance. Stage 3 (risk_eval): Computes composite_score using the weighted formula (35% 24h velocity + 15% device churn + 50% vector similarity) plus the circuit-breaker override: if max_vec_sim >= 0.92, GREATEST(...) immediately elevates the score to max_vec_sim (>= 0.92), guaranteeing that any transaction matching a known fraud signature is blocked even if the account has zero prior spending today. Stage 4 (inserted_tx): Inserts the transfer into payment_ledger with decision = 'BLOCKED' (>= 0.85), 'FLAGGED_GREY_ZONE' (0.60..0.8499), or 'APPROVED' (< 0.60). Stage 5 (outbox_enqueue): Conditionally inserts a 12-field JSONB forensic payload into agent_triage_outbox when decision = 'FLAGGED_GREY_ZONE', returning (tx_id, composite_risk_score, decision, outbox_id) to the caller in one atomic transaction. 7.2 Detailed Breakdown of the Python Classes (src/) src/benchmark/feature_generator.py: Synthetic Traffic, UUIDv7, and 64-D Vector Math UUIDv7Generator: Generates time-ordered 128-bit UUIDs (RFC 9562 UUIDv7) where the first 48 bits store the Unix timestamp in milliseconds. Unlike random UUIDv4 keys that scatter writes across random disk pages and fragment B-Tree indexes, UUIDv7 keys append sequentially at the right edge of the B-Tree. BehavioralVectorProjector: Deterministically maps a TransactionContext into a 64-dimensional numpy.float64 vector (list[float]) normalized to unit length (||v||_2 = 1.0). It also provides perturb(base_vec, target_cosine_similarity) (exposed on the facade as create_perturbed_vector) to simulate fraud rings mutating their scripts to an exact cosine similarity around known attack centroids. RiskScoringPolicy: Encapsulates the composite risk formula and decision thresholds (APPROVED, FLAGGED_GREY_ZONE, BLOCKED), mirrored against the SQL CTE and verified by unit tests in tests/unit/test_risk_scoring_math.py. PaymentWorkloadGenerator: Orchestrates synthetic PIX/FedNow payment requests (generate_payment_request), normal and anomalous behavioral contexts (generate_random_context), and SQL parameter binding (bind_hot_path_sql and PaymentRequest.to_sql_params). src/benchmark/seeder.py: High-Speed Bulk Seeding and Engine Strategy Pattern EngineInitializerStrategy (Abstract Base Class): Defines how each database engine configures its extensions and indexes after bulk data is loaded: AlloyDBEngineInitializer: Selected via --engine-mode alloydb; executes sql/02_setup_alloydb.sql (enabling the Columnar Engine and building the alloydb_scann index), with automatic fallback to sql/03_setup_aurora_baseline.sql when run against standard PostgreSQL. FROM STDIN") in 25,000-row batches, runs ANALYZE so the query planner and SCaNN k-means quantizer have fresh statistics, and invokes the chosen EngineInitializerStrategy. src/benchmark/runner.py: Asynchronous 500 TPS Runner and Plan/Recall Evaluators DatabaseStatsCollector and DatabaseBlockCounters: Query pg_stat_database before and after the timed run to compute the exact shared_buffer_hit_ratio delta. GenAISDKStrategy: Calls Gemini 4 Hydrogen (gemini-4-hydrogen) via the google-genai Python SDK with response_mime_type="application/json" and validates the response via AgentAssessment. DeterministicLocalStrategy: Evaluates payloads locally without cloud credentials for offline testing and continuous integration (and automatically serves as a safe fallback if a remote AI call fails). AgentTriageWorker.process_once: Executes the three-phase cycle: Phase 1 (Claim): Reclaims stale leases older than 30 seconds (clearing lease_token), claims a batch of PENDING rows with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, sets status = 'PROCESSING' and lease_token = gen_random_uuid(), and commits immediately (< 2 ms) so no row locks are held during AI inference. Phase 2 (Infer): Runs FraudInferenceStrategy.evaluate completely outside any database transaction (~3.5 s live measured on Vertex AI gemini-4-hydrogen). Phase 3 (Immunize): Calls complete_triage_and_immunize to execute a fenced UPDATE (AND status = 'PROCESSING' AND lease_token = $2::UUID) marking the outbox row 'COMPLETED' (aborting if rowcount == 0 to block zombie overwrites) and, when verdict == 'CONFIRMED_FRAUD' and confidence_score >= 0.85, inserts the 64-D vector into fraud_signatures (source = 'GEMINI_AGENT_IMMUNIZED') with the >= 0.98 cosine deduplication check. src/benchmark/reporter.py: Telemetry Aggregator and Markdown/CSV Exporter CsvTelemetryExporter and MarkdownReportFormatter: Aggregate the telemetry JSON files (--inputs) and generate results/benchmark_summary.md and results/raw_telemetry.csv. There Are No Dumb Questions Q: Why does the code use UUIDv7 instead of the famous UUIDv4 to give every payment an ID? A: UUIDv4 is 100% random — it's like shoving new sheets into random pages of a binder, constantly splitting and scrambling the B-Tree index! UUIDv7 starts with the exact millisecond timestamp, so every new payment appends neatly at the end of the binder — much faster to write and search. 8. Step-by-Step Guide: Choose Your Own Adventure! You don't need a cloud account to play with this project! Pick the path that fits your time: 10 seconds (no Docker, no cloud): run the tests and rebuild the report from our archived live cloud data (Step 8.2). 5 minutes on your laptop: spin up AlloyDB Omni for free in Docker (Step 8.3). Full cloud race: provision Google Cloud AlloyDB and AWS Aurora with Terraform (Steps 8.4 & 8.5). 8.1 Prerequisites Python 3.11+ Docker and Docker Compose (allocate at least 10 GB of RAM in Docker Desktop settings so the container can reserve 4gb of shared memory, shm_size, and 4096 MB for the local Columnar Engine) Terraform >= 1.5 (only required when deploying the cloud clusters on Google Cloud and AWS) Copy the environment configuration template (which sets default DSN connection URLs, where DSN stands for Data Source Name, the standard URL containing the database username, password, host address, and port): cp .env.example .env Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode 8.2 Step 1: Run the Automated Tests and Generate Reports Offline (Takes 10 Seconds) You can verify all code, risk math, and report generators immediately on your machine without starting Docker or cloud clusters: python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate pip install -e ".[dev]" # Run the automated unit & integration tests and linter pytest -v ruff check src/ tests/ # Consolidate the 12 live cloud JSON files into results/benchmark_summary.md and results/raw_telemetry.csv python -m src.benchmark.reporter \ --inputs "./results/gcp_live/run_*.json" "./results/aws_live/run_*.json" \ --output-dir ./results Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode 8.3 Step 2: Run Locally with AlloyDB Omni (Docker Compose) AlloyDB Omni is the downloadable Docker container edition of Google Cloud AlloyDB that runs locally on your laptop and includes the Columnar Engine and alloydb_scann. Start the local AlloyDB Omni 16 container: make up-local Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Seed 200,000 ledger rows and 25,000 fraud signatures: make seed-local Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Run the 500 TPS benchmark suite across 50%, 5%, and 0.5% selectivities: make benchmark-local Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Run the autonomous triage worker: Local deterministic mode (no API key needed, processes one batch and exits): make worker-local Live Gemini 4 Hydrogen via Google GenAI SDK: export GEMINI_API_KEY="your-api-key" export GEMINI_MODEL_ID="gemini-4-hydrogen" python -m src.agent.triage_worker \ --dsn "postgresql://postgres:postgres@localhost:5432/postgres" \ --agent-mode genai_sdk \ --model-id gemini-4-hydrogen \ --once Shut down the local container when finished: make down-local Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode 8.4 Step 3: Run on Google Cloud (AlloyDB 4 vCPU / 32 GB + Vertex AI Gemini 4 Hydrogen) Provision the AlloyDB cluster and co-located c3-standard-4 VM: gcloud auth application-default login cd terraform/gcp_alloydb terraform init terraform apply \ -var="project_id=YOUR_GCP_PROJECT_ID" \ -var="region=us-central1" \ -var="db_password=YOUR_SECURE_DB_PASSWORD" Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Connect to the c3-standard-4 VM (gcloud compute ssh), clone this repository, install dependencies (pip install -e .), read the private IP from terraform output, then seed and run the ablation suite: export PG_DSN="postgresql://postgres:YOUR_SECURE_DB_PASSWORD@<ALLOYDB_PRIMARY_IP>:5432/postgres" python -m src.benchmark.seeder \ --dsn "$PG_DSN" \ --engine-mode alloydb \ --ledger-rows 2000000 \ --signature-rows 500000 for MODE in alloydb_row_hnsw alloydb_col_hnsw alloydb_col_scann; do python -m src.benchmark.runner --dsn "$PG_DSN" --mode "$MODE" --tps 500 --duration 60 done python -m src.agent.triage_worker --dsn "$PG_DSN" --agent-mode in_db_ml --model-id gemini-4-hydrogen Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode 8.5 Step 4: Run the AWS Aurora PostgreSQL 16 Parity Test (db.r7g.xlarge I/O-Optimized) Provision the AWS Aurora I/O-Optimized (PostgreSQL 16.14) cluster and c7g.xlarge EC2 load generator (an AWS virtual server accessed via AWS SSM, Systems Manager, a secure terminal without opening SSH port 22): cd terraform/aws_aurora terraform init terraform apply \ -var="aws_region=us-east-2" \ -var="engine_version=16.14" \ -var="db_password=YOUR_SECURE_DB_PASSWORD" Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Connect to the c7g.xlarge instance via AWS SSM, clone the repo, install (pip install -e .), grab the endpoint from terraform output, and run aurora_io_hnsw: export AURORA_DSN="postgresql://postgres:YOUR_SECURE_DB_PASSWORD@<AURORA_WRITER_ENDPOINT>:5432/postgres" python -m src.benchmark.seeder \ --dsn "$AURORA_DSN" \ --engine-mode aurora \ --ledger-rows 2000000 \ --signature-rows 500000 python -m src.benchmark.runner \ --dsn "$AURORA_DSN" \ --mode aurora_io_hnsw \ --tps 500 \ --duration 60 \ --output-dir ./results python -m src.benchmark.reporter --inputs "./results/run_*.json" --output-dir ./results Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Tear down both cloud environments right after collecting telemetry: make destroy-cloud Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Final Bullet Points (To Keep in Your Pocket) Reflex + Brain: never stall a 50 ms payment waiting 3.5 s for an AI model — let the database react in milliseconds while Gemini 4 Hydrogen vaccinates the database in the background. Columnar Engine + alloydb_scann: on identical 4 vCPU / 32 GB hardware (2.5M rows), AlloyDB delivered 5.3x higher TPS, 5.9x lower p99, and 100% fraud accuracy vs. 67.3% on AWS Aurora. 9. blocks.html_en: Imagine you are standing at a bakery counter and you pay for your coffee using an instant transfer on your phone, like PIX in Brazil or FedNow in the United States.

There Are No Dumb Questions

Q: Wait a minute... if Gemini is so smart, why doesn't the bank just ask the AI on every single payment?
A: Because deep thinking takes time! In our live test on Google Cloud Vertex AI (Google Cloud's managed AI platform, locations/global endpoint), asking Gemini 4 Hydrogen to investigate a suspicious transaction took 3,543.6 ms (~3.5 seconds). If the bank waited 3.5 seconds on every cup of coffee, the bakery line would wrap around the block and the payment would time out.

Q: Then what is the problem with traditional cloud databases like AWS Aurora?
A: CPU and memory traffic jams! Traditional databases store all data line by line inside one shared RAM area. When the database tries to scan 40,000 payments from the last 24 hours while running filtered vector searches, the processor clogs up and payments per second collapse.

Transactions Per Second (TPS) measures how many payments hit the database every second. Throughout our benchmark, we fire 500 operations every second (500 TPS) nonstop: 450 payment authorizations per second plus 50 new fraud signatures inserted per second.

blocks.html_en: Every payment is saved in a table called payment_ledger (the bank's official notebook) using ACID transactions. ACID stands for Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability, which is the database's all-or-nothing safety guarantee: either the entire payment is recorded cleanly on disk, or nothing is changed at all. Under the hood, PostgreSQL enforces this using two mechanisms: a Write-Ahead Log (WAL), which is a sequential crash-recovery diary written to disk before any table page changes, and Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC), which keeps row snapshots so readers and writers never block one another.

blocks.html_en: Normally, an application talks to a database in several back-and-forth network trips: first asking for the 24-hour total, waiting for the answer, then asking for matching fraud patterns, waiting again, and finally saving the payment. Each trip across the network wastes milliseconds. In our project, we use a SQL Common Table Expression (CTE, written with WITH ... AS) inside sql/queries/hot_path_authorize.sql to bundle all five steps into a single instruction. The application makes one trip to the database and gets the final decision back in milliseconds.

blocks.html_en: 2.4 64-Dimensional Vectors (vector(64)) and Cosine Similarity (<=>)

sentences.en: 2.4 64-Dimensional Vectors (vector(64)) and Cosine Similarity (<=>)

blocks.html_en: How does a database know whether a new payment behaves like a scam? We take behavioral clues from the transaction (such as transfer amount relative to the user's norm, time of night, device change frequency, implied travel speed, and merchant category) and convert them into a list of 64 numbers. That list of 64 numbers is called a 64-Dimensional Vector Embedding (vector(64)).

sentences.en: How does a database know whether a new payment behaves like a scam?

We take behavioral clues from the transaction (such as transfer amount relative to the user's norm, time of night, device change frequency, implied travel speed, and merchant category) and convert them into a list of 64 numbers.
That list of 64 numbers is called a 64-Dimensional Vector Embedding (vector(64)).

blocks.html_en: Geometrically, you can picture that 64-number list as an arrow pointing in a specific direction in space. When we compare the current payment's arrow against a confirmed scam's arrow using PostgreSQL's Cosine Distance operator (<=>), the database measures the angle between the two arrows. We convert that distance into Cosine Similarity (1.0 - distance): a score of 1.0 means the two payments point in the exact same behavioral direction (a 100% match), while 0.0 means they are orthogonal (unrelated).

• HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World): Think of HNSW as a multi-story subway network built over your vectors:
    • Multiple Floors: The top floor has a few "express stations" (m = 16 links per node); the ground floor connects every fraud vector to its closest local neighbors like city streets.
    • Fast Navigation: The database hops along express stations to reach your payment's neighborhood, then drops to the ground floor to grab the 10 closest neighbors.

• Why HNSW Breaks Under Strict SQL Filters (0.5%) and Heavy Writes (50 TPS):
    1. Filter Blindness (Post-Filtering): HNSW's web only knows angles — it has no idea which merchant_category or selectivity_bucket each node belongs to. Under a 0.5% filter, 99.5% of visited nodes go straight into the trash. Its candidate queue (ef_search = 40) runs dry before collecting 10 valid frauds: in our live AWS Aurora run, Recall@10 dropped to 67.3% (0.6733) at p99 = 567.21 ms (and turning on hnsw.iterative_scan to keep walking deeper degrades latency even further).
    2. Lock Contention at 50 TPS: Every new fraud vector forces HNSW to search across layers (build parameter ef_construction = 64), lock neighboring nodes, and rewire up to m = 16 edges.

sentences.en: What alloydb_scann Is and How It Solves Both Problems

blocks.html_en: alloydb_scann is AlloyDB's native vector index powered by SCaNN (Scalable Nearest Neighbors), the Google Research algorithm behind Google Search, YouTube, and Google Play. It stands on three pillars:

sentences.en: alloydb_scann is AlloyDB's native vector index powered by SCaNN (Scalable Nearest Neighbors), the Google Research algorithm behind Google Search, YouTube, and Google Play.
It stands on three pillars:

blocks.html_en: • Tree-Quantized Partitioning (num_leaves): Instead of tangling vectors in a hard-to-update spiderweb, alloydb_scann sorts them into organized folders ("leaves", such as num_leaves = 100 for 500k vectors) around center points (centroids) learned via k-means clustering. A new fraud drops straight into its folder with zero web rewiring.

sentences.en: Tree-Quantized Partitioning (num_leaves): Instead of tangling vectors in a hard-to-update spiderweb, alloydb_scann sorts them into organized folders ("leaves", such as num_leaves = 100 for 500k vectors) around center points (centroids) learned via k-means clustering.
A new fraud drops straight into its folder with zero web rewiring.

blocks.html_en: • Anisotropic Vector Quantization and sq8 Compression: Anisotropic quantization preserves the arrow's angle (what matters for Cosine Similarity <=>), instead of naive uniform rounding. Meanwhile, sq8 shrinks each 32-bit float into an 8-bit integer — 4x smaller, fitting straight inside the CPU's SIMD cache.

sentences.en: Anisotropic Vector Quantization and sq8 Compression: Anisotropic quantization preserves the arrow's angle (what matters for Cosine Similarity <=>), instead of naive uniform rounding.
Meanwhile, sq8 shrinks each 32-bit float into an 8-bit integer — 4x smaller, fitting straight inside the CPU's SIMD cache.

blocks.html_en: • Single-Stage Bitmap Pre-Filtering: Relational columns (merchant_category, selectivity_bucket) use a B-Tree (PostgreSQL's balanced sorted tree index). alloydb_scann grabs the B-Tree's bitmap (a compact binary 1 = keep, 0 = skip checklist) and intersects it with SCaNN's leaves before measuring any angles — skipping 99.5% of irrelevant rows and delivering 100% Recall@10 in 0.29 ms on our live 2.5M-row run.

blocks.html_en: 2.6 Lock-Free Queue (FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) and google_ml_integration

sentences.en: 2.6 Lock-Free Queue (FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) and google_ml_integration

blocks.html_en: When a borderline payment lands in agent_triage_outbox, multiple background AI workers poll it at the same time. Each row stores its forensic snapshot in JSONB (PostgreSQL's binary-indexed JSON format). With FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, workers never block each other: if Worker #1 grabs Row #1, Worker #2 jumps straight to Row #2 in zero microseconds. The worker then invokes Gemini 4 Hydrogen on Vertex AI via google_ml_integration (google_ml.predict_row) or the Google GenAI Python SDK (Software Development Kit).

Bullet Points (What You Just Mastered in Section 2)

  • HTAP + CTE: doing both the cashier's job (save 1 payment) and the manager's job (sum 40,000 receipts) at once, in one single trip to the database.

  • FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED: a traffic-jam-free queue so multiple AI workers can grab cases in parallel.

Sharpen Your Pencil (15-Second Lightning Challenge!)

Imagine a scammer opens a brand-new mule account today. They have spent $0 in the last 24 hours (V_24h = 0) and are using just 1 phone (D_24h = 1/5 = 0.2), but their behavioral arrow matches a scam Gemini discovered yesterday by 95% (S_vec = 0.95).

  1. What would the risk score be without the 0.92 circuit breaker?
  2. What is the risk score with the 0.92 circuit breaker?

blocks.html_en:
There Are No Dumb Questions

Q: Why expand 6 clues into 64 numbers when 6 numbers already sound like enough?
A: Because scams hide in the combination of clues (for example, spending big at 3:00 AM plus impossible 900 km/h travel). Expanding into 64 dimensions with sine/cosine waves and cross-products lets a simple angle comparison inside the database spot those curved combinations without calling a heavy neural network!

Q: Does the database freeze while waiting ~3.5 seconds for Gemini?
A: Never! In Phase 1 (< 2 ms), the worker marks the row 'PROCESSING' and closes the database transaction before calling Gemini. While Gemini thinks in the cloud, zero rows are locked and live payments keep flying through.

Bullet Points (Section 3 Math in 3 Lines)

  • 6 clues → 64 numbers (length 1.0): turns behavior into a directional arrow ready for angle checks inside the database.
  • 0.92 circuit breaker: stops a brand-new mule account from slipping past with zero 24-hour spending history.
  • Gemini vaccine (~3.5 s offline): investigates grey-zone cases with zero DB locks and writes the new signature with >= 0.98 deduplication.

blocks.html_en: When we compare Google Cloud AlloyDB and AWS Aurora PostgreSQL 16, we never rely on a simple "average" response time. Averages hide tail spikes: if 99 payments finish in 5 milliseconds and 1 payment freezes for 5 full seconds, the average looks fine, even though customers are experiencing timeouts.

Averages hide tail spikes: if 99 payments finish in 5 milliseconds and 1 payment freezes for 5 full seconds, the average looks fine, even though customers are experiencing timeouts.

blocks.html_en: • p50 Latency (The Median Customer): Imagine lining up 100 payments from fastest (#1) to slowest (#100). p50 is the time of payment #50 right in the middle. When p50 = 5.60 ms (local AlloyDB Omni) or 26.71 ms (4-vCPU cloud stress test at 486 TPS), half of all payments finished in that time or less.

blocks.html_en: • Recall@10 (Scam Detection Accuracy): After the load test, the runner executes filtered vector queries twice: once using the vector index (alloydb_scann or pgvector HNSW), and once with indexes turned off (SET LOCAL enable_indexscan = off) so PostgreSQL checks every row to find the true 10 closest fraud vectors. Recall@10 is the overlap between the two lists: 1.00 means the index caught 10 out of the 10 real frauds, whereas 0.67 means the index missed roughly 1 in 3 real frauds.

blocks.html_en:
There Are No Dumb Questions

Q: Wait a second! If a single AlloyDB query took ~5.1 ms, why is p99 in the cloud table 95.54 ms?
A: Picture a supermarket cashier who scans your items in 5 seconds. If 1 shopper arrives at a time, you're out in 5 seconds! But if 32 shoppers sprint to the same cashier at the exact same instant (our 500 TPS stress test on just 4 vCPU), the last person in line waits for the people ahead. The wild part is that on the exact same 4 vCPUs, AlloyDB handled 486 TPS (p99 = 95.54 ms) while AWS Aurora jammed at 92.2 TPS (p99 = 567.21 ms)! With 8 vCPU in production (or 200 TPS on 4 vCPU), the queue vanishes and p99 stays right under 20 ms.

Q: How did alloydb_scann get faster when the SQL filter got stricter (212.31 ms at 50% → 95.54 ms at 0.5%)?
A: Because bitmap pre-filtering shrinks the pile before measuring any vector angles! It's like hunting for a rare trading card: if someone first hands you only the 2,500 holographic cards (0.5%) instead of 250,000 (50%), you find the right one way faster — and without missing a single match (100% Recall@10).

blocks.html_en: Running the full 2.5M-row benchmark on managed Google Cloud AlloyDB 16.14 surfaced four practical tweaks that delivered a 12.7x per-query speedup:

blocks.html_en:
• Use now(), never clock_timestamp(), in Columnar Engine filters:
    • The Trap: clock_timestamp() is VOLATILE (re-evaluated per row), blocking SIMD pushdown.
    • The Fix & Payoff: Switching to now() - INTERVAL '24 hours' (STABLE) unlocked "Columnar cache search mode": "native".

blocks.html_en:
• Split COUNT(DISTINCT) out of the columnar aggregation (12.7x speedup):
    • The Trap: Counting distinct devices inside the 40,050-row scan forced a 3.4 MB in-memory quicksort (64.8 ms).
    • The Fix & Payoff: Splitting sql/queries/hot_path_authorize.sql into corridor_stats (pure SIMD AVG in 4.24 ms, 0 shared buffer hits) + sender_velocity (Index Only Scan in 0.11 ms) cut isolated query time to ~5.1 ms.

blocks.html_en:
There Are No Dumb Questions

Q: Do I have to spend $1,000 to reproduce this benchmark in my own account?
A: Not at all! Because cloud billing is hourly and we tear everything down right after with make destroy-cloud, running the full lab for 2 hours costs roughly $2.93 on GCP and $1.74 on AWS — under $5.00 total!

Q: Why did AlloyDB save $133,570 over 3 years in Scenario C?
A: Two reasons working together: (1) the Columnar Engine + alloydb_scann give AlloyDB 5.3x more TPS per vCPU, so it only needs 8 vCPUs where Aurora needs 32 vCPUs; and (2) Google Cloud's 3-Year CUD gives ~51.5% off with $0 upfront.

Bullet Points (The Final Scoreboard from Section 5)

  • Performance (4 vCPU / 32 GB, 0.5% filter): AlloyDB delivered 5.3x higher TPS (486.0 vs. 92.2), 5.9x lower p99 (95.54 ms vs. 567.21 ms), and 100% vs. 67.3% fraud accuracy.
  • Production Costs (~500 TPS with HA, 3-Year Commit): AlloyDB 8 vCPU HA costs $34,845 over 3 years ($967.93/mo, $0 upfront) vs. $168,415 over 3 years ($4,678.21/mo amortized) on AWS Aurora — $133,570 saved (-79.3%, 4.8x cheaper)!

sentences.en: The Entity-Relationship (ER) diagram below shows the three tables inside the database (PAYMENT_LEDGER, AGENT_TRIAGE_OUTBOX, and FRAUD_SIGNATURES), every column and data type, which columns are accelerated by the AlloyDB Columnar Engine and alloydb_scann, and how they connect during the self-immunizing loop:

blocks.html_en:
• sql/01_schema.sql: The Three Core Tables

    • payment_ledger: Stores every instant transfer (tx_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, sender_account_id, receiver_account_id, device_fingerprint, merchant_category, selectivity_bucket, amount_cents, tx_timestamp, behavioral_vec vector(64), composite_risk_score, and decision).
    • fraud_signatures: Stores confirmed 64-D fraud patterns (signature_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, merchant_category, selectivity_bucket, created_at, source in 'SEED_CORPUS' | 'CHURN_STREAM' | 'GEMINI_AGENT_IMMUNIZED', behavioral_vec vector(64), and pattern_description).
    • agent_triage_outbox: Stores suspicious grey-zone payments (outbox_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY, tx_id with ON DELETE CASCADE, status in 'PENDING' | 'PROCESSING' | 'COMPLETED' | 'FAILED', lease_token UUID for fencing stale workers, payload JSONB, agent_verdict, agent_rationale, created_at, and processed_at) along with a partial index idx_outbox_pending_poll (WHERE status IN ('PENDING', 'PROCESSING')) so background workers find pending items and recover stalled leases in sub-millisecond time.

• sql/02_setup_alloydb.sql: AlloyDB Columnar Engine and alloydb_scann Setup

    • Loads alloydb_scann, google_columnar_engine, and google_ml_integration.
    • Creates the shared B-Tree indexes (idx_ledger_velocity_btree, idx_ledger_sender_24h, and idx_fraud_sig_filters) and builds idx_fraud_sig_scann: CREATE INDEX idx_fraud_sig_scann ON fraud_signatures USING scann (behavioral_vec cosine) WITH (num_leaves = 100, quantizer = 'sq8');.
    • Configures 8 database-level SCaNN parameters via ALTER DATABASE postgres SET (including scann.vector_node_min_dimensionality = 32, scann.custom_scan_replace_prefilter = on, scann.num_leaves_to_search = 15, and scann.pre_reordering_num_neighbors = 50) to enable single-stage bitmap pre-filtering (Custom Scan (vector scan)), and calls SELECT google_columnar_engine_add('public.payment_ledger', ...) to pin the analytical columns in the SIMD columnar cache.

• sql/queries/hot_path_authorize.sql: Inside the 5-Stage Single-Trip CTE

    • Stage 1 (corridor_stats + sender_velocity -> velocity_window): Separates the 24-hour corridor average (corridor_stats using now() - INTERVAL '24 hours' for pure SIMD Columnar Engine aggregate pushdown) from the sender's individual 24-hour velocity (sender_velocity using Index Only Scan on idx_ledger_sender_24h for sum_24h_cents, tx_count_24h, and distinct_devices_24h).
    • Stage 2 (vector_anomaly): Queries fraud_signatures with WHERE merchant_category = $3 AND selectivity_bucket <= $4 ORDER BY behavioral_vec <=> $2::vector(64) LIMIT 10, converting cosine distance into similarity 1.0 - distance.
    • Stage 3 (risk_eval): Computes composite_score using the weighted formula (35% 24h velocity + 15% device churn + 50% vector similarity) plus the circuit-breaker override: if max_vec_sim >= 0.92, GREATEST(...) immediately elevates the score to max_vec_sim (>= 0.92), guaranteeing that any transaction matching a known fraud signature is blocked even if the account has zero prior spending today.
    • Stage 4 (inserted_tx): Inserts the transfer into payment_ledger with decision = 'BLOCKED' (>= 0.85), 'FLAGGED_GREY_ZONE' (0.60..0.8499), or 'APPROVED' (< 0.60).
    • Stage 5 (outbox_enqueue): Conditionally inserts a 12-field JSONB forensic payload into agent_triage_outbox when decision = 'FLAGGED_GREY_ZONE', returning (tx_id, composite_risk_score, decision, outbox_id) to the caller in one atomic transaction.

• src/benchmark/feature_generator.py: Synthetic Traffic, UUIDv7, and 64-D Vector Math

    • UUIDv7Generator: Generates time-ordered 128-bit UUIDs (RFC 9562 UUIDv7) where the first 48 bits store the Unix timestamp in milliseconds. Unlike random UUIDv4 keys that scatter writes across random disk pages and fragment B-Tree indexes, UUIDv7 keys append sequentially at the right edge of the B-Tree.
    • BehavioralVectorProjector: Deterministically maps a TransactionContext into a 64-dimensional numpy.float64 vector (list[float]) normalized to unit length (||v||_2 = 1.0). It also provides perturb(base_vec, target_cosine_similarity) (exposed on the facade as create_perturbed_vector) to simulate fraud rings mutating their scripts to an exact cosine similarity around known attack centroids.
    • RiskScoringPolicy: Encapsulates the composite risk formula and decision thresholds (APPROVED, FLAGGED_GREY_ZONE, BLOCKED), mirrored against the SQL CTE and verified by unit tests in tests/unit/test_risk_scoring_math.py.
    • PaymentWorkloadGenerator: Orchestrates synthetic PIX/FedNow payment requests (generate_payment_request), normal and anomalous behavioral contexts (generate_random_context), and SQL parameter binding (bind_hot_path_sql and PaymentRequest.to_sql_params).

• src/benchmark/runner.py: Asynchronous 500 TPS Runner and Plan/Recall Evaluators

    • DatabaseStatsCollector and DatabaseBlockCounters: Query pg_stat_database before and after the timed run to compute the exact shared_buffer_hit_ratio delta.
    • ExplainPlanAnalyzer: Executes EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, FORMAT JSON) outside the timed loop and inspects the JSON plan tree to confirm Custom Scan (Columnar Scan) and idx_fraud_sig_scann vs. idx_fraud_sig_hnsw.
    • RecallEvaluator: Measures Recall@10 across probe vectors per selectivity bucket (500, 50, 5) by comparing index results against exact brute-force ground truth (SET LOCAL enable_indexscan = off; SET LOCAL enable_bitmapscan = off;).
    • HTAPBenchmarkRunner: Before every columnar run, executes VACUUM payment_ledger and google_columnar_engine_refresh('public.payment_ledger'); uses psycopg_pool.AsyncConnectionPool to sustain 500 TPS (90% hot_path_authorize.sql executions + 10% fraud_signatures churn inserts with source = 'CHURN_STREAM'), measures Recall@10 with num_probes = 15, and records p50, p95, and p99 latencies into a validated BenchmarkResult Pydantic model.

• src/agent/triage_worker.py: Three-Phase Lock-Free Autonomous Agent

    • OutboxRepository: Handles all SQL operations on agent_triage_outbox and fraud_signatures (reclaim_stale_leases, claim_pending_batch, and complete_triage_and_immunize).
    • FraudInferenceStrategy (Strategy Pattern, where each class provides a swappable way to call the AI):
      • InDatabaseVertexAIStrategy: Calls Gemini 4 Hydrogen from inside AlloyDB using SELECT google_ml.predict_row(model_id => 'gemini-4-hydrogen', ...).
      • GenAISDKStrategy: Calls Gemini 4 Hydrogen (gemini-4-hydrogen) via the google-genai Python SDK with response_mime_type="application/json" and validates the response via AgentAssessment.
      • DeterministicLocalStrategy: Evaluates payloads locally without cloud credentials for offline testing and continuous integration (and automatically serves as a safe fallback if a remote AI call fails).
    • AgentTriageWorker.process_once: Executes the three-phase cycle:
      1. Phase 1 (Claim): Reclaims stale leases older than 30 seconds (clearing lease_token), claims a batch of PENDING rows with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, sets status = 'PROCESSING' and lease_token = gen_random_uuid(), and commits immediately (< 2 ms) so no row locks are held during AI inference.
      2. Phase 2 (Infer): Runs FraudInferenceStrategy.evaluate completely outside any database transaction (~3.5 s live measured on Vertex AI gemini-4-hydrogen).
      3. Phase 3 (Immunize): Calls complete_triage_and_immunize to execute a fenced UPDATE (AND status = 'PROCESSING' AND lease_token = $2::UUID) marking the outbox row 'COMPLETED' (aborting if rowcount == 0 to block zombie overwrites) and, when verdict == 'CONFIRMED_FRAUD' and confidence_score >= 0.85, inserts the 64-D vector into fraud_signatures (source = 'GEMINI_AGENT_IMMUNIZED') with the >= 0.98 cosine deduplication check.

There Are No Dumb Questions

Q: Why does the code use UUIDv7 instead of the famous UUIDv4 to give every payment an ID?
A: UUIDv4 is 100% random — it's like shoving new sheets into random pages of a binder, constantly splitting and scrambling the B-Tree index! UUIDv7 starts with the exact millisecond timestamp, so every new payment appends neatly at the end of the binder — much faster to write and search.

Final Bullet Points (To Keep in Your Pocket)

  • Reflex + Brain: never stall a 50 ms payment waiting 3.5 s for an AI model — let the database react in milliseconds while Gemini 4 Hydrogen vaccinates the database in the background.
  • Columnar Engine + alloydb_scann: on identical 4 vCPU / 32 GB hardware (2.5M rows), AlloyDB delivered 5.3x higher TPS, 5.9x lower p99, and 100% fraud accuracy vs. 67.3% on AWS Aurora.

content_html_zh:
1. Starting from Zero: The 50-Millisecond Coffee Mystery

Imagine you are standing at a bakery counter and you pay for your coffee using an instant transfer on your phone, like PIX in Brazil or FedNow in the United States.

Between the moment your finger taps "Send" and the moment the card machine beeps "Payment Approved", less than one-twentieth of a second passes (about 50 milliseconds). To picture how fast that is, a single human eye blink takes 300 milliseconds. In other words, the entire payment has to finish six times faster than a blink!

Inside that tiny fraction of a blink, the bank's database has only 15 to 20 milliseconds to finish three completely different jobs at the exact same time:

  1. Lock the transfer in the vault safely: Write down who sent the money, who received it, and the exact amount, making sure not a single cent disappears or gets duplicated even if someone pulls the power plug mid-transfer.
  2. Check the last 24 hours of spending in that business category (the "payment corridor"): Glance at roughly 40,000 recent transfers in that specific type of store (merchant_category, like bakeries versus car dealerships), add them up, and calculate the average to check whether the amount makes sense or an intruder is draining the account.
  3. Hunt for known scams in real time: Fraud rings run automated bots that leave subtle "fingerprints" (phone model, late-night hours, device switching, internet network). The database must compare the current payment against a catalog of 500,000 confirmed scams, while 50 brand-new scams per second are being added to that catalog at the exact same time.

There Are No Dumb Questions Q: Wait a minute... if Gemini is so smart, why doesn't the bank just ask the AI on every single payment? A: Because deep thinking takes time! In our live test on Google Cloud Vertex AI (Google Cloud's managed AI platform, locations/global endpoint), asking Gemini 4 Hydrogen to investigate a suspicious transaction took 3,543.6 ms (~3.5 seconds). If the bank waited 3.5 seconds on every cup of coffee, the bakery line would wrap around the block and the payment would time out. Q: Then what is the problem with traditional cloud databases like AWS Aurora? A: CPU and memory traffic jams! Traditional databases store all data line by line inside one shared RAM area. When the database tries to scan 40,000 payments from the last 24 hours while running filtered vector searches, the processor clogs up and payments per second collapse.

1.1 The Big Idea: Two-Speed Architecture (Just Like Your Body!)

Have you ever accidentally touched a hot pan? Your hand pulls back before your brain even finishes thinking "ouch, that's hot!". That happens because your body runs at two speeds: an ultra-fast reflex in your spine and deep detective thinking in your brain.

We built that exact same design inside Google Cloud AlloyDB for PostgreSQL and tested it head-to-head against AWS Aurora PostgreSQL 16.14 on identical 4 vCPU / 32 GB machines (4 virtual CPU cores and 32 gigabytes of RAM) with 2,500,000 rows:

  1. Speed 1 (~5.1 ms per query — The Spinal Reflex): The database itself runs the 24-hour corridor math, compares the payment against 500,000 known scams, and safely locks the transfer in ~5.1 ms (measured via EXPLAIN ANALYZE, PostgreSQL's built-in "X-ray & stopwatch" — comfortably inside the 15–20 ms budget). Honest payments breeze through; known scams are blocked on the spot.
  2. Speed 2 (~3.5 s in the background — The Detective Brain): When a payment lands in the "grey zone" (not obviously honest, yet not matching any old scam), the database drops a copy into an internal waiting tray. A background worker picks it up without slowing down a single customer, asks Gemini 4 Hydrogen on Vertex AI (locations/global) to investigate, and when Gemini confirms a brand-new scam, writes its mathematical "fingerprint" right back into the database. Seconds later, Speed 1 blocks that new attack all by itself — the database literally self-immunizes!

2. Understanding Every Concept Before We Look at the Numbers

Before we open the benchmark tables, let's unpack every technical piece using everyday analogies — with zero unexplained jargon.

2.1 Milliseconds (ms), Throughput (TPS), and ACID Ledger Writes

A millisecond (ms) is one-thousandth of a second (1,000 ms = 1 second). Our strict budget for the database is under 20 ms. Transactions Per Second (TPS) measures how many payments hit the database every second. Throughout our benchmark, we fire 500 operations every second (500 TPS) nonstop: 450 payment authorizations per second plus 50 new fraud signatures inserted per second.

Every payment is saved in a table called payment_ledger (the bank's official notebook) using ACID transactions. ACID stands for Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability, which is the database's all-or-nothing safety guarantee: either the entire payment is recorded cleanly on disk, or nothing is changed at all. Under the hood, PostgreSQL enforces this using two mechanisms: a Write-Ahead Log (WAL), which is a sequential crash-recovery diary written to disk before any table page changes, and Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC), which keeps row snapshots so readers and writers never block one another.

2.2 OLTP, OLAP, HTAP, and Single-Trip SQL (CTE)

In database engineering, workloads usually fall into two camps:

  • OLTP (Online Transaction Processing) is like a supermarket cashier scanning one carton of milk: fast, tiny individual writes (INSERT one PIX transfer).
  • OLAP (Online Analytical Processing) is like the store manager asking for the average price across 40,000 receipts from the last 24 hours (SUM and AVG over 40,000 rows).
  • HTAP (Hybrid Transactional and Analytical Processing) means doing both the cashier's job and the manager's job inside the same database at the exact same instant, without copying data to a separate analytics server first.

Normally, an application talks to a database in several back-and-forth network trips: first asking for the 24-hour total, waiting for the answer, then asking for matching fraud patterns, waiting again, and finally saving the payment. Each trip across the network wastes milliseconds. In our project, we use a SQL Common Table Expression (CTE, written with WITH ... AS) inside sql/queries/hot_path_authorize.sql to bundle all five steps into a single instruction. The application makes one trip to the database and gets the final decision back in milliseconds.

2.3 RAM, Shared Buffer Hit Ratio, and the AlloyDB Columnar Engine (SIMD)

Think of RAM (Memory) as your kitchen countertop, and Disk (Storage) as a basement pantry two flights of stairs down. Grabbing an ingredient already sitting on the countertop is instant; walking down to the basement takes ages. PostgreSQL keeps its most active data in 8-kilobyte blocks on that countertop, an area called the Shared Buffer Pool (shared_buffers).

The Shared Buffer Hit Ratio (%) shows how often, out of every 100 reads, the data was already sitting on the countertop (RAM) without walking down to the basement (Disk). In our live cloud test with 32 GB of RAM, all 2.5 million rows fit in memory on both engines (99.99%–100.0% hit ratio). Yet AWS Aurora still stalled at 92.2 TPS (p99 = 567.21 ms) while AlloyDB flew at 486.0 TPS (p99 = 95.54 ms)!

为什么？ Because of the structural difference between a Row Store and the AlloyDB Columnar Engine:

Imagine a paper ledger with 40,050 lines, where each line holds 10 pieces of information (Transaction ID, Sender, Receiver, Device Code, Category, Timestamp, Amount, 64-Number Vector...):

  • Row Store (AWS Aurora): Standard PostgreSQL reads every full line just to sum the Amount column. Even when everything sits in RAM, the CPU burns almost all its cycles skipping over IDs, device codes, and vectors across 40,050 rows per payment — and on larger-than-RAM datasets, those scans also evict hot payment pages from memory.
  • AlloyDB Columnar Engine (google_columnar_engine): AlloyDB carves out an isolated columnar cache in RAM (8 GB on the cloud cluster; 4 GB in local Docker) storing only the math columns (amount_cents, merchant_category, tx_timestamp) stacked vertically side by side.
  • SIMD Superpower: With numbers packed side by side, the CPU uses SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) circuits (such as AVX-512 on Intel/AMD and ARM NEON on Apple Silicon/Graviton) to sum 8 to 16 values in one clock tick. In live EXPLAIN ANALYZE on 2.5M rows, AlloyDB summed 40,050 rows in 4.24 ms with 0 shared buffer hits!

2.4 64-Dimensional Vectors (vector(64)) and Cosine Similarity (<=>)

How does a database know whether a new payment behaves like a scam? We take behavioral clues from the transaction (such as transfer amount relative to the user's norm, time of night, device change frequency, implied travel speed, and merchant category) and convert them into a list of 64 numbers. That list of 64 numbers is called a 64-Dimensional Vector Embedding (vector(64)).

Geometrically, you can picture that 64-number list as an arrow pointing in a specific direction in space. When we compare the current payment's arrow against a confirmed scam's arrow using PostgreSQL's Cosine Distance operator (<=>), the database measures the angle between the two arrows. We convert that distance into Cosine Similarity (1.0 - distance): a score of 1.0 means the two payments point in the exact same behavioral direction (a 100% match), while 0.0 means they are orthogonal (unrelated).

2.5 What Is alloydb_scann and Why Does pgvector HNSW Struggle When We Filter Data?

In a real bank, you never search across all fraud vectors blindly; you combine the vector search with a SQL Filter (for example: "Only compare this payment against fraud vectors in merchant category #3 and within risk bucket <= 5").

The percentage of rows that survive that SQL filter is called Selectivity:

  • At 50% Selectivity (selectivity_bucket <= 500), half the table passes the filter.
  • At 5% Selectivity (selectivity_bucket <= 50), only 1 out of 20 rows passes.
  • At 0.5% Selectivity (selectivity_bucket <= 5), only 1 out of 200 rows passes the filter.

Checking hundreds of thousands of vectors one by one is too slow, so databases use a Vector Index. This is where AWS Aurora (pgvector HNSW) and Google Cloud AlloyDB (alloydb_scann) take completely different paths:

What Is pgvector HNSW, How Does It Work, and Where Does It Break?

Before we compare the two vector indexes, let's understand what pgvector and HNSW mean:

  • pgvector is the open-source extension that adds vector storage (vector(64)) and similarity search to standard PostgreSQL and AWS Aurora.
  • HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World): Think of HNSW as a multi-story subway network built over your vectors: Multiple Floors: The top floor has a few "express stations" (m = 16 links per node); the ground floor connects every fraud vector to its closest local neighbors like city streets. Fast Navigation: The database hops along express stations to reach your payment's neighborhood, then drops to the ground floor to grab the 10 closest neighbors.
  • Why HNSW Breaks Under Strict SQL Filters (0.5%) and Heavy Writes (50 TPS): Filter Blindness (Post-Filtering): HNSW's web only knows angles — it has no idea which merchant_category or selectivity_bucket each node belongs to. Under a 0.5% filter, 99.5% of visited nodes go straight into the trash. Its candidate queue (ef_search = 40) runs dry before collecting 10 valid frauds: in our live AWS Aurora run, Recall@10 dropped to 67.3% (0.6733) at p99 = 567.21 ms (and turning on hnsw.iterative_scan to keep walking deeper degrades latency even further). Lock Contention at 50 TPS: Every new fraud vector forces HNSW to search across layers (build parameter ef_construction = 64), lock neighboring nodes, and rewire up to m = 16 edges.

What alloydb_scann Is and How It Solves Both Problems

alloydb_scann is AlloyDB's native vector index powered by SCaNN (Scalable Nearest Neighbors), the Google Research algorithm behind Google Search, YouTube, and Google Play. It stands on three pillars:

  1. Tree-Quantized Partitioning (num_leaves): Instead of tangling vectors in a hard-to-update spiderweb, alloydb_scann sorts them into organized folders ("leaves", such as num_leaves = 100 for 500k vectors) around center points (centroids) learned via k-means clustering. A new fraud drops straight into its folder with zero web rewiring.

  1. Anisotropic Vector Quantization and sq8 Compression: Anisotropic quantization preserves the arrow's angle (what matters for Cosine Similarity <=>), instead of naive uniform rounding. Meanwhile, sq8 shrinks each 32-bit float into an 8-bit integer — 4x smaller, fitting straight inside the CPU's SIMD cache.

  1. Single-Stage Bitmap Pre-Filtering: Relational columns (merchant_category, selectivity_bucket) use a B-Tree (PostgreSQL's balanced sorted tree index). alloydb_scann grabs the B-Tree's bitmap (a compact binary 1 = keep, 0 = skip checklist) and intersects it with SCaNN's leaves before measuring any angles — skipping 99.5% of irrelevant rows and delivering 100% Recall@10 in 0.29 ms on our live 2.5M-row run.

2.6 Lock-Free Queue (FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) and google_ml_integration

When a borderline payment lands in agent_triage_outbox, multiple background AI workers poll it at the same time. Each row stores its forensic snapshot in JSONB (PostgreSQL's binary-indexed JSON format). With FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, workers never block each other: if Worker #1 grabs Row #1, Worker #2 jumps straight to Row #2 in zero microseconds. The worker then invokes Gemini 4 Hydrogen on Vertex AI via google_ml_integration (google_ml.predict_row) or the Google GenAI Python SDK (Software Development Kit).

Bullet Points (What You Just Mastered in Section 2) HTAP + CTE: doing both the cashier's job (save 1 payment) and the manager's job (sum 40,000 receipts) at once, in one single trip to the database. SIMD Columnar Engine: stores only the math columns vertically in RAM and adds 8 to 16 numbers per CPU tick without crowding out payment memory. alloydb_scann vs. HNSW: HNSW walks blindly and throws away 99% of nodes on SQL filters; alloydb_scann applies a bitmap pre-filter before measuring angles. FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED: a traffic-jam-free queue so multiple AI workers can grab cases in parallel.

3. Deep Dive: The Exact Mathematical and Vector Models Used to Detect Fraud

A critical question for both data scientists and engineers is: What exact mathematical model generates the 64-dimensional vectors, how are attack mutations simulated, and what exact equations decide if a payment is fraudulent?

We do not use random dummy numbers. In src/benchmark/feature_generator.py and sql/queries/hot_path_authorize.sql, fraud detection is governed by five explicit mathematical steps that run in < 0.2 ms on the client and ~5.1 ms per isolated query (< 15 ms in production on 8 vCPU) inside the database.

3.1 Mathematical Step 1: The 6 Raw Behavioral Signals (TransactionContext)

Before a payment touches the database, we extract 6 core mathematical signals (written in mathematical notation as x ∈ ℝ⁶, meaning a list x of 6 real decimal numbers) that summarize the physics and behavior of the transfer:

  1. x₁ = velocity_ratio (24h Spending Acceleration): How fast the account is spending today divided by its normal daily average (Normal customer: 0.1 to 1.2; Fraudulent attack: 2.5 to 6.0).
  2. x₂ = sin(2π · hour / 24) and x₃ = cos(2π · hour / 24) (Cyclical Time-of-Day Encoding): Why use Sine and Cosine for hours? In plain numbers, 23:59 (hour 23) and 00:01 (hour 0) look 23 hours apart, even though they are only 2 minutes apart in the middle of the night. Mapping the 24-hour clock onto a unit circle using (sin θ, cos θ) guarantees that late-night scam hours sit right next to each other geometrically.
  3. x₄ = amount_zscore (Statistical Z-Score of the Transfer Amount vs. the Business Category / "Corridor"): What is a "Payment Corridor"? In banking, a corridor (merchant_category, numbered 1..50 in our database) simply means the specific type of business or payment channel: for example, a bakery or coffee shop (where the 24-hour average transfer μ_corridor is $15) versus a car dealership (where the 24-hour average is $25,000). Sending $8,000 at a car dealership is normal, but sending $8,000 at a bakery is a major anomaly. The Z-Score measures how many standard deviations (σ, the typical spread of values around the average) the current payment amount is above the normal 24-hour average (μ_corridor) of that specific business category:

(Normal customer: -0.8 to +1.1; Fraudulent attack: +2.0 to +5.5 standard deviations above that category's norm).

  1. x₅ = geo_velocity_delta (Physical Travel Speed / "Impossible Travel" in km/h): The implied physical speed (distance divided by time) between the IP/GPS location of the user's previous transfer and the current one (Normal customer: 0 to 40 km/h; Fraudulent attack via VPN or emulator jump across states/countries: 300 to 950 km/h).
  2. x₆ = graph_degree (24h Fan-Out / Device and Receiver Multiplicity): How many distinct hardware devices and receiver accounts have interacted with this sender in the last 24 hours (Normal customer: 1.0 to 2.5; Mule or account-takeover ring: 4.0 to 12.0).

3.2 Mathematical Step 2: Non-Linear 64-D Feature Expansion (BehavioralVectorProjector.project)

Think of this step like a music equalizer: we take 6 simple notes (the 6 clues above) and blend them into 64 rich chords. 为什么？ Because fraud rings hide in the combination of signals (like a huge amount at 3:00 AM plus impossible travel). Expanding into 64 numbers (v ∈ ℝ⁶⁴), inspired by Random Fourier Features (RFF) and Second-Order Polynomial Kernel Expansion, lets a single Cosine Distance (<=>) inside PostgreSQL "hear" those curved combinations without calling a heavy neural network:

  1. Dimensions 0..47 (48 Multi-Frequency Fourier Harmonics): For each of the 4 harmonic wave frequencies f ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4}, we compute both the sine and cosine of all 6 core signals scaled by 0.5 · f:

Why this works mathematically: By Bochner's theorem, expanding raw numbers into sine and cosine waves lets a simple dot product (Cosine Similarity) approximate a Gaussian RBF kernel (a smooth curved decision boundary from machine learning), turning curved boundaries into flat geometric angles.

  1. Dimensions 48..63 (16 Second-Order Cross-Terms and Hyperbolic Tangent Activations): 6 Pairwise Behavioral Interactions (Dims 48..53): Multiply risk factors in pairs to capture joint spikes:
  • 6 Time-of-Night Cross-Modulations (Dims 54..59): Cross the sine and cosine of the transaction hour with spending velocity, amount Z-score, and geographic travel speed:
  • 4 Non-Linear Saturating Activations (Dims 60..63): Apply the Hyperbolic Tangent (tanh, a smooth S-shaped curve that squashes any extreme number into [-1.0, +1.0]) so a single outlier cannot dominate all 64 dimensions:

  1. L2 Unit-Hypersphere Normalization (Every Arrow Has Length 1.0): Picture shrinking or stretching every arrow so they all have the exact same length (1.0), making only their direction matter when comparing. We divide r by its Euclidean length ||r||₂:

With length 1.0, the Cosine Similarity between an incoming payment v̂ and a stored fraud signature ŝ inside alloydb_scann is the cosine of the angle θ between them:

Here is the exact Python implementation from src/benchmark/feature_generator.py:

def project(self, ctx: TransactionContext) -> np.ndarray:
    angle = 2.0 * np.pi * (ctx.hour_of_day / 24.0)
    base = np.array([
        ctx.velocity_ratio,
        np.sin(angle),
        np.cos(angle),
        ctx.amount_zscore,
        ctx.geo_velocity_delta / 100.0,
        ctx.graph_degree / 5.0,
    ], dtype=np.float32)

    # Dims 0..47: 4 harmonic frequencies x 6 signals x (sin, cos) = 48 Fourier features
    raw = np.empty(64, dtype=np.float32)
    idx = 0
    for freq in (1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0):
        raw[idx : idx + 6] = np.sin(0.5 * freq * base); idx += 6
        raw[idx : idx + 6] = np.cos(0.5 * freq * base); idx += 6

    # Dims 48..63: 6 pairwise products + 6 night modulations + 4 tanh/trig saturations
    v, s, c, z, g, d = base
    raw[48:54] = [v * z, v * g, v * d, z * g, z * d, g * d]
    raw[54:60] = [s * v, c * v, s * z, c * z, s * g, c * g]
    raw[60:64] = [np.tanh(v + z), np.tanh(g + d), np.sin(v * d), np.cos(z * g)]

    # L2 Unit-Hypersphere Normalization (||v||_2 = 1.0 -> cosine similarity = dot product)
    return raw / (np.linalg.norm(raw) + 1e-12)

3.3 Mathematical Step 3: Gram-Schmidt Orthogonal Perturbation (BehavioralVectorProjector.perturb)

How do we test whether the database catches a fraudster who tweaks their bot to be exactly 96% (0.96) or 78% (0.78) similar to a known scam û? Think of the drawing below as using a 90° L-ruler and a protractor: first we find a perpendicular arrow (û⊥), then we blend both arrows in the exact ratio to tilt to the target angle!

Instead of adding unpredictable random noise, BehavioralVectorProjector.perturb(base_vec, target_cosine_similarity) applies Gram-Schmidt Orthogonalization in 3 steps:

  1. Draw a random 64-number vector z ~ N(0, I₆₄) (64 numbers sampled from a standard normal bell curve with mean 0 and standard deviation 1).
  2. Subtract its projection onto û and normalize to get a unit arrow û⊥ at an exact 90-degree angle (û · û⊥ = 0):

  1. Blend both arrows using the exact target cosine α = cos(θ):

Because cos²(θ) + sin²(θ) = 1, v̂_mutated stays length 1.0 with an exact Cosine Similarity of α (to 6 decimal places) against û.

def perturb(self, base_vec: np.ndarray, target_cosine_similarity: float) -> np.ndarray:
    u = base_vec / (np.linalg.norm(base_vec) + 1e-12)
    z = self._rng.standard_normal(u.shape).astype(np.float32)
    p = z - float(np.dot(z, u)) * u                      # Gram-Schmidt orthogonal component
    u_perp = p / (np.linalg.norm(p) + 1e-12)             # Unit vector at exact 90 degrees
    alpha = float(np.clip(target_cosine_similarity, -1.0, 1.0))
    mutated = alpha * u + np.sqrt(max(0.0, 1.0 - alpha * alpha)) * u_perp
    return (mutated / (np.linalg.norm(mutated) + 1e-12)).astype(np.float32)

3.4 Mathematical Step 4: The Piecewise Hybrid Risk Scoring Equation (hot_path_authorize.sql and RiskScoringPolicy)

Inside Stage 3 (risk_eval) of sql/queries/hot_path_authorize.sql, the database combines the 24-hour Columnar Engine aggregates and the alloydb_scann top-10 vector similarity into the final risk score R ∈ [0.0, 1.0] using a Piecewise Linear + Non-Linear Circuit-Breaker Equation:

Where each term is defined as:

  • V_24h = min(1.0, sum_24h_cents / 5,000,000) (Weight 0.35): Reaches its maximum of 1.0 when the sender's 24-hour cumulative spend in that merchant corridor reaches $50,000 (5,000,000 cents).
  • D_24h = min(1.0, distinct_devices_24h / 5.0) (Weight 0.15): Reaches its maximum of 1.0 when 5 or more distinct hardware device fingerprints touch the account within 24 hours.
  • S_vec = max_{k=1..10}(1.0 - (behavioral_vec <=> sig_k)) (Weight 0.50): The highest cosine similarity among the top-10 pre-filtered fraud signatures returned by alloydb_scann.
  • I(S_vec >= 0.92) · S_vec (The Self-Immunizing Circuit Breaker): Here I(condition) is an indicator function (a simple on/off switch that equals 1 if the condition inside the parentheses is true, and 0 if it is false). Notice why this switch is essential: suppose a brand-new mule account has $0 spent in the last 24 hours (V_24h = 0) and only 1 device (D_24h = 0.2). Without the circuit breaker, even if its vector matched a confirmed fraud signature at S_vec = 0.95, the weighted sum alone would be 0.35(0) + 0.15(0.2) + 0.50(0.95) = 0.505, which would mistakenly approve the fraud. Because of the max(I(S_vec >= 0.92) · S_vec, ...) override, any vector match >= 0.92 bypasses the low velocity weights and jumps straight to R = 0.95 >= 0.85 (BLOCKED).

Here is the exact atomic 4-stage SQL CTE executed on every payment authorization (sql/queries/hot_path_authorize.sql):

WITH corridor_stats AS (
    -- Stage 1a: Pure SIMD Columnar Engine pushdown (4.24 ms, 0 shared buffer hits)
    SELECT COALESCE(AVG(amount_cents)::DOUBLE PRECISION, 0.0) AS corridor_avg_cents
    FROM payment_ledger
    WHERE merchant_category = $4 AND created_at >= now() - INTERVAL '24 hours'
),
sender_velocity AS (
    -- Stage 1b: B-Tree Index Only Scan on idx_ledger_sender_24h (0.11 ms)
    SELECT COALESCE(SUM(amount_cents), 0) AS sum_24h_cents,
           COUNT(*) AS tx_count_24h,
           COUNT(DISTINCT device_fingerprint) AS distinct_devices_24h
    FROM payment_ledger
    WHERE sender_id = $1 AND created_at >= now() - INTERVAL '24 hours'
),
vector_search AS (
    -- Stage 2: alloydb_scann Iterative Pre-Filtered Cosine Search (0.29 ms, 100% Recall@10)
    SELECT COALESCE(MAX(1.0 - (behavioral_vec <=> $6::vector(64))), 0.0) AS max_vec_sim
    FROM (
        SELECT behavioral_vec FROM fraud_signatures
        WHERE merchant_category = $4 AND selectivity_bucket <= $7
        ORDER BY behavioral_vec <=> $6::vector(64)
        LIMIT 10
    ) top_k
),
risk_eval AS (
    -- Stage 3: Weighted Score + Self-Immunizing Circuit Breaker (>= 0.92 overrides!)
    SELECT LEAST(1.0, GREATEST(
        CASE WHEN vs.max_vec_sim >= 0.92 THEN vs.max_vec_sim ELSE 0.0 END,
        0.35 * LEAST(1.0, sv.sum_24h_cents / 5000000.0)
        + 0.15 * LEAST(1.0, sv.distinct_devices_24h / 5.0)
        + 0.50 * vs.max_vec_sim
    )) AS composite_score
    FROM sender_velocity sv CROSS JOIN vector_search vs
)
INSERT INTO payment_ledger (...)
SELECT ...,
       CASE
           WHEN composite_score >= 0.85 THEN 'BLOCKED'
           WHEN composite_score >= 0.60 THEN 'FLAGGED_GREY_ZONE'
           ELSE 'APPROVED'
       END AS decision
FROM risk_eval ...;

4. What Is Analyzed in the Benchmark? (p50, p95, p99, Recall@10, and Buffer Hit Ratio)

When we compare Google Cloud AlloyDB and AWS Aurora PostgreSQL 16, we never rely on a simple "average" response time. Averages hide tail spikes: if 99 payments finish in 5 milliseconds and 1 payment freezes for 5 full seconds, the average looks fine, even though customers are experiencing timeouts.

Instead, our benchmark runner (src/benchmark/runner.py) analyzes five concrete metrics on every run:

  1. p50 Latency (The Median Customer): Imagine lining up 100 payments from fastest (#1) to slowest (#100). p50 is the time of payment #50 right in the middle. When p50 = 5.60 ms (local AlloyDB Omni) or 26.71 ms (4-vCPU cloud stress test at 486 TPS), half of all payments finished in that time or less.
  2. p95 Latency (Peak Traffic Stability): p95 is payment #95 in that line of 100. When p95 = 9.09 ms (local AlloyDB Omni) or 73.99 ms (4-vCPU cloud stress test), 95 out of every 100 payments finished in that time or less.
  3. p99 Latency (The Worst-Case 1% Tail That Central Banks Enforce): p99 is payment #99 out of 100, representing the slowest 1% of requests when the database is under full 500 TPS stress. Instant payment networks like PIX enforce strict service-level agreements on p99.
  4. Recall@10 (Scam Detection Accuracy): After the load test, the runner executes filtered vector queries twice: once using the vector index (alloydb_scann or pgvector HNSW), and once with indexes turned off (SET LOCAL enable_indexscan = off) so PostgreSQL checks every row to find the true 10 closest fraud vectors. Recall@10 is the overlap between the two lists: 1.00 means the index caught 10 out of the 10 real frauds, whereas 0.67 means the index missed roughly 1 in 3 real frauds.
  5. Shared Buffer Hit Ratio (RAM Efficiency): Measured directly from PostgreSQL's pg_stat_database catalog (blks_hit vs. blks_read), showing what percentage of page reads came straight from RAM without touching disk storage.
Bullet Points (How to Read Any Benchmark Like a Pro) Ignore simple averages: always look at p99 — it tells you whether the unluckiest 1% of customers are stuck waiting at the checkout counter. Speed without accuracy is useless: answering in 5 ms doesn't help if Recall@10 is 0.67 and 1 out of every 3 real scams slips through the net!

5.4 Four "Aha!" Engineering Clues Discovered on Managed AlloyDB

Beginner Note: This subsection is an optional deep dive for database engineers (DBAs). If you are new to databases, feel free to jump straight to Section 5.5 (Costs) without missing a beat!

Running the full 2.5M-row benchmark on managed Google Cloud AlloyDB 16.14 surfaced four practical tweaks that delivered a 12.7x per-query speedup:

  1. Use now(), never clock_timestamp(), in Columnar Engine filters: The Trap: clock_timestamp() is VOLATILE (re-evaluated per row), blocking SIMD pushdown. The Fix & Payoff: Switching to now() - INTERVAL '24 hours' (STABLE) unlocked "Columnar cache search mode": "native".
  2. Split COUNT(DISTINCT) out of the columnar aggregation (12.7x speedup): The Trap: Counting distinct devices inside the 40,050-row scan forced a 3.4 MB in-memory quicksort (64.8 ms). The Fix & Payoff: Splitting sql/queries/hot_path_authorize.sql into corridor_stats (pure SIMD AVG in 4.24 ms, 0 shared buffer hits) + sender_velocity (Index Only Scan in 0.11 ms) cut isolated query time to ~5.1 ms.
  3. Set scann.vector_node_min_dimensionality = 32 for 64-D vectors: The Trap: Single-stage bitmap pre-filtering defaults to vectors with >= 100 dimensions. The Fix & Payoff: Setting min_dimensionality = 32 + custom_scan_replace_prefilter = on unlocked Bitmap assisted pre-filtering in 0.29 ms at 100% Recall@10.
  4. Run VACUUM ANALYZE before populating the Columnar Engine: The Trap: Bulk COPY rows must be marked all-visible to load 100% into columnar stripes. The Fix & Payoff: VACUUM ANALYZE loaded 96,777 / 96,777 blocks into columnar stripes; on managed AlloyDB, use ALTER DATABASE ... SET (instead of ALTER SYSTEM SET) and google_ml.create_model(..., model_auth_type => 'alloydb_service_agent_iam').

Before looking at the numbers, learn 3 cloud-billing words in 15 seconds:

  • 1 Node (Zonal) vs. HA (2 Nodes): with 1 node, if that server fails, the database goes down; with HA (High Availability), two nodes work as a pair — if one fails, the standby takes over automatically.

To compare apples to apples, we spread the upfront across all 36 months: Amortized Monthly Cost = (Upfront + 36 × Monthly) ÷ 36.

6.1 Inside the AlloyDB Cluster (Everything Runs In-Database on the Hot Path)

Notice in the diagram below that AlloyDB never calls an external data warehouse (like BigQuery) or an external vector service during a payment. The OLTP Row Store, the Columnar Engine, the alloydb_scann index, and the agent_triage_outbox table all live inside the same AlloyDB for PostgreSQL cluster. Only the asynchronous worker reaches out to Vertex AI (Gemini 4 Hydrogen).

6.2 The Self-Immunizing Loop (~5.1 ms Spinal Reflex vs. ~3.5 s Cortical Agent)

Trace the diagram below with your finger across three lanes: on the top lane, a mutated scam lands in the grey zone in milliseconds; on the middle lane, the Python worker calls Gemini 4 Hydrogen (~3.5 s) with zero DB locks and writes the 64-D "vaccine"; on the bottom lane, seconds later, the next attack slams into the green shield and gets blocked automatically!
